Having a hard Tim finding a niche

I'd start reaching out to other people who might have gear. Put an ad up on a crewing site for your next project. What will happen is 1: You'll discover other talented people who can bring their own flair to your work 2: You'll get free gear 3: You instantly build up your audience because it's more than 1 person who wants to get the word out, it's now every crew member spreading the word of their project. 4: You can't do everything yourself. The more helping hands you have, the stronger your project gets.

This is a bad idea. If you had friends who do that sort of thing it's one thing, but to ask complete strangers to come contribute their time and gear for free is dumb and annoying and it devalues what film makers do.

I disagree 100%. I'm making headway in the industry only because I've networked and met new people. Now I'm able to produce a film from scratch and fill out a crew list in 2 hours because I have a fantastic sense of who does what and is good at what in my town. I also get regularly called to be on set because I put myself out there so much by working on a variety of different projects with people I'd never met.

I think it's one thing to work for free to learn stuff and network, that's not a bad idea and OP should consider it. Making a call for people to come loan their time, talent and gear when you haven't quite figured out how things work is another thing. There's a lot OP can do to learn how things work before he goes about finding a crew to help him. Hell maybe he can put out a call to work on a few projects and ask that in exchange they help him with his project. That's a more than fair trade-off and one that I so rarely see.

Ahh, that's actually a better way of putting it; I appreciate you adding that. It's true, my networking has been me going on sets in order for me to learn my way before asking for other people to work on my stuff. Thank you.

You don't need a fucking Canon DSLR to make good films (technically speaking or otherwise; a Canon DSLR is still a low-end camera). You just need to know the limits of your camera and find ways to work with it or around it. In reality your biggest problem is probably a lack of lighting (which can be cheap had for less than $50) and poor sound (a little more expensive, but you can do a lot with a cleverly placed cell phone with a recorder app or do some stuff that doesn't really have dialogue, alternatively decent field recorders can be had for under $200).

That said, both of those ideas sound boring. To answer your question - No. No one wants to watch realistic life struggles. People want to watch things with real action, real drama, real stakes. No one cares if Brian the temp turns in his work on time or not, he's still gonna have a job tomorrow. On the other hand people do care if Brian the bomb tech doesn't finish his work on time, because people are gonna fucking die if he doesn't. THAT's interesting, there's something at stake.

I can't imagine what your first project was like, but of the chronically depressed people I have been friends with, their lives are generally boring as fuck. Further if it was just one episode that tells me there was no character arc. You just introduced a character than that was it. Where's the drama? Where's the excitement? Where's the lesson? Was it funny? I don't get it, and I definitely wouldn't watch it based on the plot synopsis you gave.

As for the second one, I did stand up for 3 years. Open mics are painfully boring. There might be some drama there but if it was about you then I doubt there was anything there either. Again the problem of only doing one episode so there's no character arc, no journey, no story. Why do I care? About local comedians telling their jokes to a room full of other comedians who have already heard them a dozen times and aren't listening anyway because they're too busy talking shit on other comedians. and Again, a poor plot synopsis that doesn't even remotely interest me.

Here's what you need to do -

1) Take a good look at your jokes. Are there any that can become sketches? If so great! Make that. If not? Well shit, there's a few books on sketch writing. I personally found "Comedy Writing for Late Night TV" to be a great resource. Some parts might not apply, but there's a lot of good shit in there.

2) Post the 2 videos you already have done on critique forums. You may get a lot of helpful advice.

3) Find better ways to sell your films, and while you're at better ways to write. One resource that's really good is "Save The Cat!" it's a book that helps dissect a lot of popular movies, why they work, what beats they hit and how you can use their formula to create unique new works. In addition there's a great part about writing a log-line (which is the first part of the process) so that your pitch is something people actually want to see.

Finally, stop attributing your success and failures to your view counts and public reception. At this stage you should only care about one thing: How many projects you finish. You're gonna make a lot of crap to start with, but do you think your favorite band just came out swinging? Probably not. Every member of that band was probably in 2 or 3 shit bands and they probably wrote a dozen cringe-worthy songs as a band before they even started writing that album you love. No one just gets into film-making and makes great movies right from the start unless they have enough money to pay the people that could probably make a better film without that guy. It takes time. Don't get hard on yourself, just get to work and make more shit, eventually you'll crap out something great.

This is absolutely fantastic advice. Most importantly recognizing that at this point in your career, you WILL make complete crap. Here is one of the first things I made. It's appalling. Here is the latest thing I produced. Progress happens, and it's ok that things don't take off the way you want them to. That's why I think it's good to bring in other perspectives. If you want people to be excited by your stuff, then run your stuff by other people before you make it. Do THEY like the sound of it? They're an audience member just like the public are audience members. If you find people willing to share a vision, then collaboration can only elevate you to that next level you're after.
